sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — was one of the smallest stegosaurs, measuring less than four meters in length despite being an adult.
This individual reached approximately 4.00 meters in length, stood 1.80 meters high, and weighed about 1 tonne.
A skeleton model in the Chongqing Municipal museum depicts the animal with fourteen pairs of plates that transformed into spikes towards the tail.
The tail appears to show at least five spikes, suggesting more than the traditional two pairs found on the limb.
Although Chungkingosaurus was quadrupedal, it could rear up on its hind legs to eat leaves from higher branches of trees.
The dorsal spikes were laterally compressed with sharp anterior and posterior edges.
Gregory S. Paul described the unique tail spike arrangement of Chungkingosaurus as a "pin-cushion array".
Fossils of Chungkingosaurus were found near Chongqing, China, starting from 1977.

In 2014, Roman Ulansky named specimen CV 00205 as Chungkingosaurus giganticus and Chungkingosaurus magnus, but Peter Malcolm Galton and Kenneth Carpenter later identified both names as dubious and referred them to C. jiangbeiensis.
Chungkingosaurus was a herbivore, like all stegosaurs.
Chungkingosaurus belongs to the class Ornithischia and its parent group is Stegosauridae.
The animal was placed within Stegosaurinae in 1983 by Dong et al., but in 2008, Maidment et al. assigned it to the family Huayangosauridae.
The form of its dermal armor makes Chungkingosaurus considered a relative of Kentrosaurus and Dacentrurus in the subfamily Kentrosaurinae.

Chungkingosaurus is a stegosaurian dinosaur from the Late Jurassic Upper Shaximiao Formation in modern-day China, living during the Late Jurassic Oxfordian stage, approximately 156 million years ago, in what is now Asia.
Other sources indicate the creature lived during the Bathonian to Callovian stages, from 168.2 to 161.5 million years ago.
Gregory S. Paul suggested in 2010 that Chungkingosaurus was the juvenile form of Tuojiangosaurus.
